subject_matter.value: Newly out of a group home, Gwen is tormented by a violent alter ego and a cold mother until she shoots the alter ego and calls her children.
subject_matter.evidence: "Get out! Just get out of here!" and "I’m going to call my children!"

literary_form.evidence: A Samuel French play with labels NELL, LOUISE and BILLIE and directions such as "rocking and flapping".

tone.evidence: Nell's hope ("She wants to be extraordinary.") against Billie's doubt.

content_warnings.evidence: Louise is "lost in her own mentally disabled word" and on medication, and in distress begins "banging her head against her chair".

difficulty.evidence: One actor switches between disabled Louise, lucid Louise and Billie, including a flashback.

performance_demands.evidence: Louise's "rocking and flapping" and sing-song voice shift to a normal tone.

audience_level.evidence: Disability and self-injury shown without graphic detail.

themes.evidence: "I don’t write the haikus . . . Louise does".

subject_matter.value: A nearly blind mother tells her skeptical daughter that her severely disabled sister composes haiku when her medicine is delayed, but the attempt to prove it ends in a screaming fit.
subject_matter.evidence: "It’s my eyes." and "She’s just repeating, Mother".

literary_form.evidence: A play from Under Thirty with labels HARRIET and THERAPIST and directions such as "pulls up the back" of her shirt.

tone.evidence: Harriet's defiance ("I got two rights") against the therapist's account of atrocities.

content_warnings.evidence: Harriet says "Cain't sell no nigga like me", the therapist recounts men who "took turns raping the twelve-year-old", a child "was already dead" and "the dogs tear my little sister to pieces", and Harriet shows whip scars: "You look at what de white man done".

difficulty.evidence: Heavy written dialect, a feigned dull act, a trance and singing.

performance_demands.evidence: Speech like "Massuh Edward done sent me", singing Go Down Moses and a narcoleptic fit.

audience_level.evidence: Rape, child deaths, slurs and torture under slavery.

themes.evidence: "I teach them how to survive." versus "Lib in de no'th or die in de South."

subject_matter.value: An enslaved Harriet Tubman is sent to a therapist who urges acceptance and reveals her own trauma, then under hypnosis gives Harriet the escape route north.
subject_matter.evidence: "You want the map? All right, Harriet Tubman, I'll give you the map".

literary_form.evidence: Emily Mann's play (Dramatists Play Service) with labels SADIE and BESSIE and shared lines marked together.

tone.evidence: Wry humor ("We are not old maids.") sits beside accounts of Jim Crow and lynching.

content_warnings.evidence: A drunk white man shouts "The nigger bitch insulted me" ("He was drunk, and he smelled bad"), and Bessie describes a lynching where men "slit her abdomen open" and "she and her unborn baby just died".

difficulty.evidence: Two voices sharing long narration, with timed joint lines.

performance_demands.evidence: Calm Sadie and fiery Bessie trade and share lines such as "Still here!"

audience_level.evidence: A graphic lynching description and racial slurs.

themes.evidence: Papa's motto that their mission "is to help somebody" runs through their story of racism and service.

subject_matter.value: Centenarian sisters Sadie and Bessie Delany recount their family, Jim Crow, lynchings and teaching in the rural South, including Bessie's near-lynching at a Georgia station.
subject_matter.evidence: "She is 101 years old, and I am 103" and the Waycross story.

literary_form.evidence: A screenplay cut with labels SKEETER, AIBILEEN, MINNY and HILLY and page cues.

tone.evidence: "You is kind." frames Aibileen's love for a child she must leave.

content_warnings.evidence: Hilly says Black maids "carry different diseases than we do", Aibileen recounts "They killed my son." and "He died right in front of me.", and Minny reports that they "set off a bomb" at Medgar Evers' house.

difficulty.evidence: Two actors cover nine roles with Southern dialect and grief.

performance_demands.evidence: Written dialect such as "I done raised seventeen kids" and business like Mae Mobley beating on the window.

audience_level.evidence: Racism, a recounted death and some profanity.

themes.evidence: "No one had ever asked me what it felt like to be me."

subject_matter.value: An aspiring writer persuades Black maids in 1963 Jackson to tell their stories for a book, which is published anonymously and costs Aibileen her job.
subject_matter.evidence: "I want to interview you" and "you are fired, Aibileen".

literary_form.evidence: A cutting of Gary E. Parker's novel (Fleming H. Revell) with added labels GLADYS and ALLIE and narrative directions.

tone.evidence: "I wish he could be here for my wedding" amid warm teasing.

content_warnings.evidence: The father "came back from Vietnam a broken man", "Suffered nightmares, sweats, the shakes" and "took to drinking, maybe some drugs too".

difficulty.evidence: Two characters move from light banter to painful questions.

performance_demands.evidence: Gladys is "reaching for the photos Allie is now holding" over her head.

audience_level.evidence: War trauma and addiction are mentioned briefly.

themes.evidence: "Maybe he left us because he loved us."

subject_matter.value: Weeks before her wedding Allie cleans out her childhood room with her mother and finds photos of the father who came back broken from Vietnam and left when she was four.
subject_matter.evidence: "It's Dad." and "a wedding in three weeks".

literary_form.evidence: A comic play from Laugh Lines with labels REBEKAH, NPO 1 and NPO 2 and directions such as "attacks her mass of thick curls".

tone.evidence: A hair police squad led by "Nap Patrol Officer Shateequa Williams" spoofs beauty pressure.

content_warnings.evidence: No sensitive content; the relaxer burn ("MY SCALP IS ON FIRE") and officers' squabbling are slapstick.

difficulty.evidence: Three roles with broad comic voices and physical struggle.

performance_demands.evidence: Written dialect such as "Giiiirrrrl, I know you did not" and Rebekah who "attacks her mass of thick curls".

audience_level.evidence: Mild profanity in a comic sketch.

themes.evidence: "you are going to be proud of your beautiful black hair-i-tage".

subject_matter.value: A biracial sixteen-year-old struggling with her curls is raided by the comic Nap Patrol, who force a painful chemical relaxer on her while preaching about heritage.
subject_matter.evidence: "Girlfriend needs a relaxer" and "I DON'T WANT STRAIGHT HAIR!"

literary_form.evidence: A Dramatists Play Service play with a CHORUS, goddesses and directions such as "With strong Southern accent."

tone.evidence: Greek-tragedy form is applied to politics, with Hillary's mantra "Emotions are stupid and I am smart".

content_warnings.evidence: Gennifer Flowers claims "We have made sweet sweet love in my bedroom" and Bill denies "sexual relations with Ms. Lewinsky".

difficulty.evidence: Two actors play chorus, goddesses, Hillary, Bill and a newscaster across decades.

performance_demands.evidence: Rapid role changes including Aphrodite speaking "With strong Southern accent."

themes.evidence: "Why can't I have both, just like men do?"

literary_form.evidence: A Smith and Kraus duo play with labels MARCIE and DENISE and directions such as "puts her arms straight down in candy cane form".

tone.evidence: Actor earnestness is mocked, as Marcie worries she is not "feeling very stripy".

content_warnings.evidence: No sensitive content; the Princess's habit to "light a cigarette" is tobacco only.

difficulty.evidence: Two comic characters build a conspiracy with physical bits.

performance_demands.evidence: Marcie "puts her arms straight down in candy cane form" while Denise plots.

audience_level.evidence: Clean comedy with mild insults.

themes.evidence: "We could overthrow her. A coup, a coup."

subject_matter.value: Two struggling actresses working a mall Christmas display plot to get the badly behaved Snow Princess fired so the understudy Snowflake can take over.

literary_form.evidence: A play from The Best Short Plays 1978 with labels FURIES, MARY and WARDER and directions such as "strains against her bonds".

tone.evidence: It ends in despair: "Damn you, God. I damn you!"

content_warnings.evidence: Mary says "My husband abuses me." and is strapped into the "Tranquilizing Chair" in "the ward fer the mentally deranged", where the warder says committal "Seems to happen more to women folks".

difficulty.evidence: One actor plays the Furies, Warder, Mrs. Lum and Stephen against Mary's escalating desperation.

performance_demands.evidence: The Warder's dialect ("I calls ye Mary"), the fragmented Furies and Mary bound as she "strains against her bonds".

audience_level.evidence: Spousal abuse, institutional cruelty and adultery.

subject_matter.value: Committed to an asylum by her husband, Mary Girard is taunted by the Furies, rebuked by her mother and rejected by her husband, and is told she will die there.
